name: PFAPA syndrome
aliases: periodic fever aphthous stomatitis pharyngitis adenitis

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: The acronym stands for periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and cervical adenitis, the defining clinical tetrad
It is the most common periodic fever syndrome of childhood, though a similar picture is increasingly recognised in adults
Fevers recur with striking clockwork regularity, and patients are typically completely well between episodes with normal growth and development
Episodes are not triggered by infection and do not respond to antibiotics
There is no identified single-gene cause, distinguishing it from the hereditary monogenic periodic fevers
Diagnosis is clinical and requires exclusion of cyclic neutropenia and the monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes
Corticosteroids given at the onset of an attack characteristically abort the fever rapidly, a response that supports the diagnosis
Colchicine may reduce attack frequency, and tonsillectomy can be curative in selected children
reference.pathophysiology: PFAPA is considered a polygenic/complex autoinflammatory disorder involving dysregulated innate immune activation, with episodic overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-1 beta during attacks. Unlike the classic hereditary periodic fevers, no single causative gene is identified, and the periodic pattern reflects intermittent inflammasome-driven inflammation rather than infection.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary periodic fever syndromes (FMF, TRAPS, HIDS, CAPS)
Adult-onset Still disease in the adult presentation
additionalInvestigations: Serial full blood counts during and between episodes to exclude cyclic neutropenia
Acute-phase reactants (elevated during attacks, normal between)
Genetic testing for monogenic periodic fevers when the presentation is atypical
Documentation of the periodicity and symptom diary
Throat swabs/cultures to confirm episodes are not infective
redFlags: Neutropenia coinciding with fevers, pointing to cyclic neutropenia rather than PFAPA
Growth failure or ill health between attacks suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Atypical features (rash, serositis, prominent arthritis) suggesting a monogenic syndrome
First presentation of a periodic fever in adulthood requiring exclusion of other systemic disease
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting in most children, typically resolving spontaneously over years with no long-term sequelae and no risk of amyloidosis; the adult form tends to be more persistent but remains non-life-threatening.
pitfalls: Repeatedly prescribing antibiotics for recurrent pharyngitis that is actually autoinflammatory
Failing to check blood counts during fevers and missing cyclic neutropenia
Assuming a childhood-only condition and overlooking adult presentations
Diagnosing PFAPA without excluding monogenic periodic fevers in atypical cases
management: Abortive single-dose corticosteroid at attack onset, which characteristically terminates the fever rapidly
Symptomatic care during episodes with antipyretics, analgesia and hydration for the pharyngitis and aphthous stomatitis
Colchicine to reduce attack frequency in patients with frequent, closely spaced episodes
Tonsillectomy as a potential definitive option in selected refractory cases
Interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra reserved for severe, treatment-resistant disease
Documentation of periodicity and exclusion of cyclic neutropenia and monogenic periodic fevers before committing to long-term therapy
Reassurance about the benign, non-life-threatening course with specialist rheumatology follow-up
